title: Measuring the Standard Electrode Potential
page_title: How to Measure Standard Electrode Potential - A level

titles.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials E⦵, Standard Cell Potentials E⦵cell & the Nernst Equation

blocks.md:
- There are three different types of half-cells that can be connected to a standard hydrogen electrode

  - A metal / metal ion half-cell
  - A non-metal / non-metal ion half-cell
  - An ion / ion half-cell (the ions are in different oxidation states)
- When a half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode, or when two half-cells are connected, a** salt bridge** is required

  - A salt bridge has **mobile ions** that complete the circuit
  - A salt bridge is typically a strip of filter paper soaked in a saturated solution of **potassium nitrate **or **potassium chloride **as nitrates and chlorides are usually soluble
  - This should ensure that no precipitates form which can affect the equilibrium position of the half-cells

- An example of a metal / metal ion half-cell is the Ag<sup>+</sup>/ Ag half-cell

  - Ag is the metal
  - Ag<sup>+</sup> is the metal ion
- This half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

- Since the Ag<sup>+</sup> / Ag half-cell has a more positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value, this is the **positive pole **and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> half-cell is the **negative** pole
- The **standard cell potential (***E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup>) is ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 0.80) - (0.00) = + 0.80 V**
- The Ag<sup>+ </sup>ions are more likely to get **reduced **than the H<sup>+</sup> ions as it has a greater *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value

  - Reduction occurs at the **positive pole**
  - Oxidation occurs at the **negative pole**

blocks.md:
- In a **non-metal / non-metal ion **half-cell **platinum **wire or foil is used as an electrode to make electrical contact with the solution

  - Like graphite, platinum is inert and does not take part in the reaction
  - The redox equilibrium is established on the platinum surface
- An example of a non-metal/non-metal ion is the Br<sub>2</sub> / Br<sup>-</sup> half-cell

  - Br is the non-metal
  - Br<sup>-</sup> is the non-metal ion
- The half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

- The Br<sub>2</sub> / Br<sup>-</sup> half-cell is the **positive pole** and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> is the **negative** pole
- ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 1.09) - (0.00) = + 1.09 V**
- The Br<sub>2</sub> molecules are more likely to get **reduced **than H<sup>+</sup> as they have a greater *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value

blocks.md:
- A **platinum electrode **is again used to form a half-cell of ions that are in **different oxidation states**
- An example of such a half-cell is the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> / Mn<sup>2+</sup> half-cell

  - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is an ion containing Mn with an oxidation number of +7
  - The Mn<sup>2+ </sup>ion contains Mn with an oxidation number of +2
- This half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

- The H<sup>+</sup> ions are also present in the half-cell as they are required to convert MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>- </sup>into Mn<sup>2+ </sup>ions
- The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> / Mn<sup>2+</sup> <sup>-</sup> half-cell is the **positive pole** and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> is the **negative** pole
- ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 1.52) - (0.00) = + 1.52 V**

blocks.name: Standard Cell Potential: Direction of Electron Flow & Feasibility

blocks.text: Standard Cell Potential: Direction of Electron Flow & Feasibility

blocks.md: - The **direction of electron flow **can be determined by comparing the *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values of two half-cells in an electrochemical cell

- The Cl<sub>2</sub> more **readily accept** electrons from the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cell

  - This is the **positive pole**
  - Cl<sub>2</sub> gets more readily reduced
- The Cu<sup>2+</sup> more **readily loses **electrons to the Cl<sub>2</sub>/Cl<sup>-</sup> half-cell

  - This is the **negative pole**
  - Cu<sup>2+ </sup>gets more readily oxidised
- The electrons flow from the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cell to the Cl<sub>2</sub>/Cl<sup>-</sup> half-cell
- The flow of electrons is from the **negative pole **to the **positive pole**

blocks.md:
- The *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values of a species indicate how **easily **they can get **oxidised **or **reduced**
- The **more **positive the value, the easier it is to reduce the species on the **left** of the half-equation

  - The reaction will tend to proceed in the **forward direction**
- The **less **positive the value, the easier it is to **oxidise** the species on the **right **of the half-equation

  - The reaction will tend to proceed in the backward direction
  - A reaction is **feasible **(likely to occur) when the *E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup> is **positive**

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md: Remember that the electrons only move through the wires in the external circuit and not through the electrolyte solution.

- The main ways to construct redox equations using the relevant half-equations:

  - Using changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations
  - Using the number of electrons for each half-cell
  
    - Both of these are discussed in the [Redox Reactions](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/chemistry/cie/25/revision-notes/6-electrochemistry/6-1-redox-processes-electron-transfer-and-changes-in-oxidation-number-oxidation-state/redox-reactions/) topic
  - Interpreting the information given to you and predicting any other chemicals involved in the reaction

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
Write the balanced chemical equation for hydrogen iodide reacting with sulfuric acid to form hydrogen sulfide, iodine and one other product

**Answer:**

- There are 2 possible methods:

  1. Using ionic half-equations
  2. Interpreting the information and predicting any other chemicals involved

**Using ionic half-equations method:**

- **Step 1:** Identify possible half-equations from the information

  - Iodide → iodine
  - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
- **Step 2:** Construct the half equations

  - Iodide → iodine
  
    - I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub>
    - This requires 2 iodide ions and 2 electrons as products to balance the equation
    - 2I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
  - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
  
    - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S
    - The 4 oxygen atoms will form 4 water molecules as products
    - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
    - The 8 hydrogen atoms in the water molecules will require 8 protons as reactants
    - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
    - The 8 protons will require 8 electrons to balance the charge
    - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
- **Step 3:** Combine the half-equations

  - Iodide → iodine
  
    - 2I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
    - The iodide half-equation needs to be multiplied by 4 to have the same number of electrons as the sulfuric acid half-equation
    - 8I<sup>–</sup> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + 8e<sup>–</sup>
  - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
  
    - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
  - Combining the half-equations
  
    - 8I<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + 8e<sup>–</sup> H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
  - Cancelling, where appropriate
  
    - The electrons cancel on both sides
    - The 8I<sup>–</sup> and 8H<sup>+</sup> can be re-written as 8HI
    - 8HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

**Interpreting and predicting method:**

- **Step 1:** Start with what you know:

  - HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + I<sub>2</sub>
- **Step 2:** Consider any elements that are not accounted for

  - The only element that is not currently considered is oxygen
- **Step 3:** Make a common and appropriate suggestion for the missing product

  - Most of these questions are in solution so there is always H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> available
  - Missing product suggestion = 4H<sub>2</sub>O
  - HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
- **Step 4:** Balance the remaining chemicals

  - 8HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
- Similar approaches can be used to balance more complicated ionic half-equations
- In these situations, you will have H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sup>+</sup>, OH<sup>-</sup> and electrons available
